name: Tsiolkovsky's Space Tower, 1895
description: Konstantin Tsiolkovsky's idea of a tower rising from the Earth's surface to geostationary height, so that a payload could reach orbit without rockets.
failedFuture: A ladder to orbit: a tower rising from the ground to geostationary height, so that people and cargo could leave the Earth without rockets. It was never built; Tsiolkovsky's was a compression tower, and the tension-cable version studied today descends from Artsutanov (1960) and Pearson (1975).
source: Tsiolkovsky, K. (1895). Грёзы о Земле и небе [Dreams of Earth and Heaven]. Wikipedia, "Space elevator".
license: Pendiente: verificar licencia de la imagen
status: Efecto presente verificado en Wikipedia (Obayashi 2012, Google X 2014, IAA 2019). Nota: la torre de Tsiolkovsky era de compresión; el cable actual desciende de Artsutanov y Pearson.

presentEffect.text: The idea survives as the space elevator. Obayashi Corporation said in 2012 that it could build one by 2050 with carbon nanotubes; in 2014 Google X shelved its effort after finding that no carbon-nanotube strand longer than a metre had been made; in 2019 the International Academy of Astronautics published 'Road to the Space Elevator Era'.

name: Project Habbakuk, 1942–1943
description: A British plan, promoted by Geoffrey Pyke, for an enormous aircraft carrier built from Pykrete, a mix of ice and wood pulp. A 60-foot scale model was tested; the project was abandoned in 1943.
failedFuture: A warship hull made of ice strengthened with wood pulp: cheap, hard to sink and independent of scarce steel. The final Habbakuk board meeting of December 1943 concluded that Habbakuk II was impractical.
source: National Interest, "Project Habakkuk: Churchill's Plan for an Aircraft Carrier Made of Ice".
license: Pendiente: verificar licencia de la imagen
status: Efecto presente verificado en Wikipedia. Año de concepción: 1942 (consulta a Pyke y Bernal); la fuente recoge además una idea de 1940 descartada como broma.

presentEffect.text: The sunken metal parts of the 1944 prototype remain in Patricia Lake, Alberta; the ice took three hot summers to melt. The material, named pykrete after Geoffrey Pyke, has been retested on television (MythBusters, 2009; BBC Bang Goes the Theory, 2010), and both hulls leaked.

name: Silbervogel, 1944
description: Eugen Sänger's design for a boost-glide spaceplane, the Silbervogel, meant to bomb New York from orbit. Designed for the German Reich; never flown.
failedFuture: A rocket-powered bomber that would skip along the upper atmosphere to strike the Americas. Sänger's 900-page proposal of 3 December 1941 was filed away for its size; a reduced version, UM 3538, was submitted in September 1944 and never built.
source: Sänger, E. (1944). Silbervogel design. Wikipedia, "Silbervogel".
license: Pendiente: verificar licencia de la imagen
status: Efecto presente verificado en Wikipedia. Año de concepción: 1941 (propuesta al RLM); el concepto se sitúa a finales de los años treinta.

presentEffect.text: Sänger's team made important progress toward regenerative cooling, in which propellant circulates around the engine bell; Wikipedia says almost all modern rocket engines use a similar design. Its lifting-body principle foreshadowed the X-20 and the Space Shuttle.

name: Black Arrow, 1964-1971
description: The British satellite launch vehicle authorised in 1964. Its last flight, R3, placed the Prospero satellite in orbit on 28 October 1971, the UK's only successful orbital launch.
failedFuture: A British route to orbit on its own rocket. Minister Frederick Corfield announced its cancellation to the Commons on 29 July 1971, because the Ministry of Defence judged the American Scout cheaper.
source: Wikipedia, "Black Arrow".
license: Pendiente: verificar licencia de la imagen
status: Sustituto verificado en Wikipedia. La ficha no da el estado actual de la órbita de Prospero.

presentEffect.text: Wikipedia notes that the UK is the only country to have developed and then abandoned a satellite launch capability. R4, which never flew, is preserved at the Science Museum in London with the Prospero flight spare, and the first stage of R3 was displayed in Penicuik, Scotland, in early 2019.

name: Ford Nucleon, 1958
description: A concept car from 1958 with a small nuclear reactor in the rear, shown by Ford as a vision of atomic transport. It was never produced.
failedFuture: A car powered by a small reactor and a steam engine instead of petrol. It premised that reactors and their shielding would one day shrink to car size; Ford showed it only as a scale model, as a vision rather than a serious design.
source: Ford Motor Company (1958). Ford Nucleon concept. Wikipedia, "Ford Nucleon".
license: Pendiente: verificar licencia de la imagen

presentEffect.text: The scale model is displayed at the Henry Ford Museum in Dearborn, Michigan. The premise has not come true: reactors able to propel a vehicle still need roughly 5 feet of shielding. The car inspired the nuclear cars of the Fallout video game franchise.

name: Project Sherwood, 1951–1958
description: The United States' secret controlled-fusion programme, begun in 1951 and declassified in 1958. Its name came from a Sherwood Forest joke about the difficulty of the problem.
failedFuture: Fusion power by magnetic confinement within a few years: a star held in magnetic bottles on Earth. In 1958 the secret programme was declassified and reorganised as basic research, losing its crash deadline.
source: Bishop, A. (1958). Project Sherwood: The U.S. Program in Controlled Fusion. Addison-Wesley. Wikipedia, "Project Sherwood".

presentEffect.text: The APS Division of Plasma Physics meetings became the International Sherwood Fusion Theory Conference, which Wikipedia says continues today. Lyman Spitzer's stellarator effort at the Princeton Plasma Physics Laboratory is tied to the programme.

name: Project Chariot, 1958–1962
description: A proposed Atomic Energy Commission plan to excavate a harbour at Cape Thompson, Alaska, with a series of nuclear explosions. Cancelled in 1962 after protests from Iñupiat communities and scientists.
failedFuture: A deep-water harbour at Cape Thompson, Alaska, to be dug with nuclear explosions as a demonstration of peaceful uses of the bomb. In 1962 the Atomic Energy Commission placed it 'in abeyance'; it was never formally cancelled.
source: U.S. Atomic Energy Commission reports on Project Chariot (1958–1962). Wikipedia, "Project Chariot".

presentEffect.text: Resistance from the village of Point Hope helped spark Native political organisation that contributed to the Alaska Native Claims Settlement Act (1971). In the early 1990s researcher Dan O'Neill found that radioactive material from a 1962 experiment had been buried at the site; in 1993 the federal government removed the contaminated soil, and in 2014 remediation of five contaminated boreholes was completed.

name: Aircraft Nuclear Propulsion, 1946–1961
description: The US programme to build a nuclear-powered bomber that could stay airborne for weeks. Engines were tested on the ground; the programme was cancelled in 1961.
failedFuture: A bomber powered by a nuclear reactor. Kennedy cancelled the programme on 26 March 1961 after about $1 billion, citing cost and the lack of a flight-worthy reactor.
source: Wikipedia, "Aircraft Nuclear Propulsion". Referencia primaria por confirmar.

presentEffect.text: The decommissioned HTRE-2 and HTRE-3 reactor assemblies are on public display at Idaho National Laboratory, beside Experimental Breeder Reactor I. The related Aircraft Reactor Experiment led to the Molten-Salt Reactor Experiment.

name: B-70 Valkyrie, 1961
description: North American's XB-70 Valkyrie, a Mach 3 bomber. Two prototypes were built; the bomber programme was cancelled in 1961, before any production aircraft existed.
failedFuture: A bomber with the payload and range of the B-52 and Mach 3 speed. Kennedy cancelled it on 28 March 1961 as 'unnecessary and economically unjustifiable' after about $800 million; two XB-70A research aircraft were completed.
source: National Museum of the U.S. Air Force, fact sheet "North American XB-70 Valkyrie".

presentEffect.text: The surviving XB-70A (AV-1) is the signature aircraft of the National Museum of the US Air Force; it was moved to the main campus in late October 2015. Its test data and materials work were used in the B-1 bomber and American supersonic transport programmes.

name: Sea Dragon, 1962
description: A design by Robert Truax for a super-heavy rocket to be built and launched from a sea platform. It was never built.
failedFuture: A rocket so large it would be built in a shipyard and fired from the sea, lifting heavy payloads at very low cost: a 1963 estimate of $59 to $600 per kilogram. Budget pressure closed the branch that studied super-heavy launchers.
source: Wikipedia, "Sea Dragon (rocket)". Referencia primaria por confirmar.

presentEffect.text: Truax's sea-launched, low-cost approach is now called a 'big dumb booster' concept. The Sea Dragon appears in the first-season finale of For All Mankind (Apple TV+, 2019), launching from the Pacific in an alternate 1983.

name: NS Savannah, 1955-1971
description: The first nuclear-powered merchant ship, proposed by Eisenhower in 1955 under Atoms for Peace and launched on 21 July 1959. Passenger service ended in 1965 and she was deactivated in 1971.
failedFuture: A nuclear merchant ship as proof that atoms could serve peace and trade. Only the Savannah was built.
source: Wikipedia, "NS Savannah".
license: Pendiente: verificar licencia de la imagen
status: Sustituto verificado en Wikipedia.

presentEffect.text: She is a National Historic Landmark (1991). Since 2008 she has been moored at the Canton Marine Terminal in Baltimore; in 2019 she was drydocked in Philadelphia for pre-decommissioning work and was back in Baltimore by early 2020. The Maritime Administration says decommissioning of her nuclear plant must be completed by 2031.

name: Project Cybersyn, 1971-1973
description: Chile's economic decision-support system under Salvador Allende, designed by Stafford Beer: a telex network (Cybernet), statistical software (Cyberstride), an economic simulator (CHECO) and an operations room (Opsroom).
failedFuture: A planned economy steered in near real time, with factories linked by telex to a control room in Santiago. By May 1973 about 26.7% of nationalised industries, half of the sector's revenue, had been included to some degree; after the coup of 11 September 1973 the military abandoned it and destroyed the operations room.
source: Wikipedia, "Project Cybersyn".

presentEffect.text: The Guardian described the network as 'a sort of socialist internet, decades ahead of its time'. Leigh Phillips and Michał Rozworski discussed it in their 2019 book, and Evgeny Morozov's 2014 essay examined its link to big data and algorithmic monitoring.
presentEffect.source: Wikipedia, "Project Cybersyn" (citing The Guardian; Phillips and Rozworski, 2019; Morozov, 2014).

name: Project Orion, 1958–1965
description: Study drawings and test models of a spacecraft driven by small nuclear explosions, developed at General Atomics between 1958 and 1965.
failedFuture: A ship pushed across the solar system by a series of nuclear explosions behind it; a 1959 NASA profile imagined a 125-day Mars round trip with eight astronauts. The Partial Test Ban Treaty of 1963 prohibited nuclear explosions in the atmosphere and in space and cut political support.
source: Dyson, G. (2002). Project Orion: The True Story of the Atomic Spaceship. Henry Holt and Company. Wikipedia, "Project Orion (nuclear propulsion)".
license: Pendiente: verificar licencia de la imagen
status: Efecto presente verificado en Wikipedia. La ficha da 1964 como año de cancelación; se mantiene 1965 de la ficha original (pendiente de confirmar).

presentEffect.text: A 26-inch wooden model, donated in 1979 by General Dynamics, is displayed at the Smithsonian's Steven F. Udvar-Hazy Center. Penn State has developed Orion-style designs (Project ICAN and AIMStar) since 1998, and Freeman Dyson's 1968 analysis of fusion-bomb Orion for Alpha Centauri remains a reference.

name: Project Pluto, 1957–1964
description: A Los Alamos programme to build a nuclear ramjet cruise missile able to fly low and at supersonic speed for hours. Cancelled in 1964.
failedFuture: A cruise missile with a nuclear ramjet, the Supersonic Low Altitude Missile, flying at about Mach 3 near the ground. Tory II-C ran at full power on 20 May 1964; Pluto was cancelled on 1 July 1964 as ICBMs advanced and doubts grew over noise and emissions.
source: Wikipedia, "Project Pluto". Referencia primaria por confirmar.

presentEffect.text: Wikipedia identifies Russia's 9M730 Burevestnik as a similar project and cites 2019 articles about its nuclear-powered cruise missile test.

name: Project Mohole, 1957–1966
description: A US project to drill through the Earth's crust beneath the ocean floor to reach the mantle, to read the planet's interior. Cancelled in 1966.
failedFuture: A hole drilled through the ocean crust to the Mohorovičić discontinuity to bring up samples of the mantle. After test drilling in 1961 off Guadalupe Island, Congress ended it in 1966 after about $57 million.
source: Wikipedia, "Project Mohole". Referencia primaria por confirmar.

presentEffect.text: Its sediment-drilling branch grew into the Deep Sea Drilling Project, and the Glomar Challenger became operational in August 1968. Phase 1 introduced dynamic positioning, now widely used, and a 2011 'Mantle Frontier' workshop shows that attempts to drill to the mantle continue.

name: Project Iceworm, 1959–1966
description: A secret US Army plan to hide up to 600 nuclear missiles in tunnels beneath the Greenland ice sheet, under cover of the Camp Century base. Cancelled in 1966.
failedFuture: A launch network for nuclear missiles hidden under the Greenland ice, built behind the cover story of Camp Century. The ice moved faster than expected; Iceworm was cancelled in 1966 and the camp closed.
source: Wikipedia, "Project Iceworm" (con referencia a Camp Century, 1959).
license: Pendiente: verificar licencia de la imagen
status: Efecto presente verificado en Wikipedia. La revista del estudio de 2016 es Geophysical Research Letters.

presentEffect.text: When the camp was decommissioned in 1967 its infrastructure and waste were left, on the assumption that snow would entomb them. They still include about 200,000 litres of diesel, PCBs and biological, chemical and radioactive waste. A 2016 study by William Colgan and colleagues in Geophysical Research Letters projected that the ice over the camp would begin melting by 2100 under current trends, potentially releasing the waste.
presentEffect.source: Wikipedia, "Project Iceworm" (citing Colgan et al., 2016, Geophysical Research Letters).

name: O'Neill's space settlements, 1975
description: Gerard O'Neill's space settlements: large cylinders, spheres and toruses housing people in orbit, designed by O'Neill with students and later with architects, planners, engineers and artists, and presented in a 1975 plan.
failedFuture: Cities in orbit as the next frontier, where people would live and work with industry in space. They remained designs.
source: Scharmen, F. (2019). CityLab.
license: Pendiente: verificar licencia de la imagen
status: Sustituto: efecto atribuido a Fred Scharmen (CityLab 2019). Bezos no atribuye él mismo la inspiración en ese artículo.

presentEffect.text: At Blue Origin's event on 9 May 2019, Jeff Bezos played a 1975 TV interview with O'Neill and Isaac Asimov and framed the choice as 'Stasis & Rationing or Dynamism & Growth'. Fred Scharmen argued in CityLab that Bezos's habitat designs closely echo O'Neill's 1975 plan, and noted that Bezos was O'Neill's student at Princeton in the mid-1980s.

name: HOTOL, 1982-1989
description: Horizontal Take-Off and Landing: a British Aerospace single-stage-to-orbit spaceplane studied from 1982 and unveiled in August 1984, aimed at launch costs of 20% of the US Space Shuttle's.
failedFuture: A plane-like launcher that would take off from a runway, reach orbit in one stage and land again. UK funding ended in 1989 and Rolls-Royce withdrew.
source: Wikipedia, "HOTOL".

presentEffect.text: After funding ended in 1989, Alan Bond, John Scott-Scott and Richard Varvill formed Reaction Engines Limited, which published its SABRE engine and Skylon concepts in 1993. Development of the core technologies was supported by ESA, the UK Space Agency, BAE and the US Air Force Research Laboratory; in 2017 the company planned a pre-cooler demonstration in 2018 and an engine-core test in 2020. It entered administration in 2024.

name: Boeing 2707, 1963–1971
description: The American supersonic transport, a swept-variable-wing airliner intended to carry passengers faster than sound. Congress withdrew funding in 1971.
failedFuture: A supersonic airliner larger than Concorde, with 122 delivery positions reserved by 26 airlines by October 1969. The Senate refused funding in March 1971 and the House voted on 20 May 1971, 215 to 204, to end it.
source: Wikipedia, "Boeing 2707". Referencia primaria por confirmar.

presentEffect.text: The final full-size mock-up survives: its forward fuselage was moved to Paine Field in Everett, Washington, in 2013 for restoration at a Museum of Flight facility. Supersonic flight over land in the US was eventually banned, and no commercial supersonic transport is in service today.

name: NERVA and Project Rover, 1959–1973
description: The US nuclear rocket programme, Project Rover and its engine NERVA. Engines were ground-tested; the programme was cancelled in 1972 and ended in 1973.
failedFuture: A nuclear thermal rocket in which a reactor heats liquid hydrogen, meant to shorten the trip to Mars. Kiwi B4E ran at 937 MW for 480 seconds in 1964; NASA announced termination on 5 January 1973 after about $1.4 billion, and no nuclear rocket flew.
source: Wikipedia, "Project Rover" and "NERVA". DOE/NNSS nuclear rocket history (2013).

presentEffect.text: On 22 May 2019 Congress approved $125 million for nuclear rocket development, and in January 2023 NASA and DARPA announced a collaboration on a nuclear thermal rocket to be tested in space. A 2013 Marshall Space Flight Center study had examined nuclear thermal engines for Mars round trips.

name: Skylab B, 1973
description: The backup space station built in case the first Skylab failed. It was never launched.
failedFuture: A second Skylab, built as a backup in 1970 and scheduled to launch between January 1975 and April 1976 to extend the Apollo-Soyuz mission by 56 to 90 days. The success of the first Skylab in May 1973 led to its cancellation.
source: Wikipedia, "Skylab B". NASA space history sources.

presentEffect.text: The backup workshop (S-IVB-515) is on display at the National Air and Space Museum in Washington, modified so that visitors can walk through the living quarters. Its S-IC-15 first stage is at the Infinity Science Center in Mississippi and the S-II-15 second stage at Johnson Space Center.

name: Aérotrain, 1965–1974
description: A French high-speed train on a cushion of air, developed by Jean Bertin. The government ended the programme in 1974.
failedFuture: A train floating on a cushion of air above a concrete track, planned to link La Défense and Cergy-Pontoise. On 5 March 1974 the I80 HV set an air-cushion speed record of 430.4 km/h; the contract was signed in June and July 1974 and then abandoned.
source: Wikipedia, "Aérotrain". Referencia primaria por confirmar.

presentEffect.text: The abandoned elevated track near Orléans still stands, visible from the Paris-Orléans railway; 120 m were demolished in 2007 for the A19 motorway, and a 20 m span was taken down in August 2015. At Gometz-le-Châtel a memorial sculpture was dedicated in July 2004 and the track became a pedestrian path in 2008-2009. The last two surviving prototypes are stored in Versailles.

name: Project Xanadu, 1960-1992
description: Ted Nelson's hypertext system, conceived in 1960 at Harvard and named in 1967 after Coleridge's 'Kubla Khan': two-way links and transclusion, in which quoted text stays connected to its source.
failedFuture: A web where every link runs both ways and quotations never lose their source. Autodesk divested the Xanadu group in 1992, and Wired called it in 1995 'the longest-running vaporware story in the history of the computer industry'.
source: Wikipedia, "Project Xanadu".

presentEffect.text: OpenXanadu was made available on the Web in 2014 as 'a working deliverable'. Nelson's mission statement criticised the Web for trivialising the original hypertext model with 'one-way ever-breaking links'.

name: Project Plowshare, 1957–1975
description: The Atomic Energy Commission's programme to find peaceful uses for nuclear explosions: harbours, canals, gas stimulation and mining. Ended in 1975.
failedFuture: Nuclear explosives as construction tools: canals dug, harbours excavated and gas freed from rock. Gnome (1961), Sedan (1962), Gasbuggy (1967), Rulison (1969) and Rio Blanco (1973) were tested; the programme ended in 1977 under public opposition, and Rio Blanco gas still carried unacceptable radionuclides.
source: U.S. Atomic Energy Commission, Project Plowshare reports. Wikipedia, "Project Plowshare". Referencia primaria por confirmar.

presentEffect.text: Tritium-contaminated water and fallout are among the lasting consequences listed. A 2009 resurgence in gas drilling brought activity close to Rulison, with 84 permits issued within 3 miles of the test site and 11 within 1 mile.

name: N1 rocket, Soviet lunar programme
description: The N1, the Soviet super-heavy rocket designed to take cosmonauts to the Moon. All four launch attempts, between 1969 and 1972, failed.
failedFuture: A Soviet super-heavy rocket to land cosmonauts on the Moon. All four uncrewed test launches between 1969 and 1972 failed; Glushko ordered it cancelled in May 1974 and the programme was formally cancelled in 1976.
source: Wikipedia, "N1 (rocket)", con datos de historias de la carrera espacial. Referencia primaria por confirmar.

presentEffect.text: The NK-33 engines built for the N1F were adapted as the AJ26 for the Antares rocket and used on the Soyuz-2.1v, first launched on 28 December 2013. In the mid-1990s Russia sold 36 engines and a production licence to Aerojet; the remains of the flight-ready N1Fs were reused as shelters and sheds around Baikonur.

name: Project Daedalus, 1973–1978
description: A British Interplanetary Society study for an unmanned fusion-powered probe to Barnard's Star, designed between 1973 and 1978.
failedFuture: An uncrewed probe that would reach Barnard's Star, 5.9 light years away, in about 50 years at around 12% of the speed of light, pushed by thermonuclear pulses. The 1978 final report stayed a design.
source: Bond, A. and Martin, A. R. (eds.) (1978). Project Daedalus. Journal of the British Interplanetary Society, Supplement. Wikipedia, "Project Daedalus".

presentEffect.text: Project Icarus, a successor study nicknamed 'Son of Daedalus', formally began on 30 September 2009. Icarus Interstellar's supervision ended in 2019 without a workable updated starship design, and a project review was published on 10 April 2020; some members moved to the Initiative for Interstellar Studies or Breakthrough Starshot.

name: Solar Power Satellite, 1979
description: NASA and the Department of Energy's 1979 studies of satellites in orbit that would collect sunlight and beam electricity to Earth by microwave.
failedFuture: Power collected in geostationary orbit and beamed to Earth by microwave, as Peter Glaser proposed in November 1968. The joint DOE/NASA study of 1978-1981 produced a reference system, but the Office of Technology Assessment found too little was known to decide whether to proceed.
source: NASA/DOE (1979). Satellite Power System Concept Development and Evaluation Program. Wikipedia, "Solar power satellite".

presentEffect.text: JAXA wirelessly beamed 1.8 kW over 50 m in March 2015; in 2019 a test base reportedly began construction in Chongqing, with a plan reported by Xinhua for a megawatt-class station by 2035; and in May 2020 the US Naval Research Laboratory conducted its first test of solar power generation in a satellite.

name: Buran, 1976-1993
description: The Soviet reusable spacecraft programme begun in 1976 in response to the US Space Shuttle. Buran made one uncrewed flight on 15 November 1988, launched on the Energia rocket.
failedFuture: A Soviet shuttle fleet with crewed flights planned for the mid-1990s. President Yeltsin terminated the programme on 30 June 1993 after about 20 billion roubles.
source: Wikipedia, "Buran programme".

presentEffect.text: A 2002 hangar roof collapse at Baikonur destroyed the only flown orbiter and killed eight workers. Other orbiters and test articles survive in museums at Speyer, Germany, and Sochi, and at Gorky Park and VDNKh in Moscow.

name: Strategic Defense Initiative, 1983
description: The US plan proposed in 1983 for a shield of lasers and interceptors in space to make nuclear missiles obsolete. It was reduced in the 1990s and no system was deployed.
failedFuture: A shield against ballistic nuclear missiles, announced by Reagan in March 1983: lasers, particle beams and orbiting interceptors. The X-ray laser and particle-beam concepts failed key tests, and in 1993 the programme was redirected to ground-based and theatre systems.
source: Wikipedia, "Strategic Defense Initiative". Referencia primaria por confirmar.

presentEffect.text: Hit-to-kill technology from the Homing Overlay Experiment and the ERIS programme fed into THAAD and the Ground-Based Interceptor of the Ground-Based Midcourse Defense system. The organisation survives as the Missile Defense Agency (renamed in 2002). Observation elements returned in 2019 through the National Defense Authorization Act, managed by the Space Development Agency.

name: Space Station Freedom, 1984-1993
description: The American space station announced by Ronald Reagan in his 1984 State of the Union address.
failedFuture: A permanent American space station, redesigned repeatedly over cost. A June 1993 House amendment to remove its funding failed by one vote, and it was merged with Russian, European and Japanese plans.
source: Wikipedia, "Space Station Freedom".

presentEffect.text: In 1993 the Alpha option was chosen, using about 75 percent of the hardware designs originally intended for Freedom, and in October 1993 NASA and the Russian Space Agency agreed to merge the projects. The first component of the resulting International Space Station was launched in 1998 and the first long-term residents arrived in November 2000.

name: Project Babylon, 1988–1990
description: An Iraqi project to build a very long-range gun, designed by Gerald Bull. Bull was murdered in 1990 and the project was stopped.
failedFuture: A gun that would have launched satellites from the ground. Its designer was shot dead in Brussels on 22 March 1990, and the gun never fired.
source: Wikipedia, "Project Babylon" and "Gerald Bull". Referencia primaria por confirmar.

presentEffect.text: Barrel sections seized by UK customs in April 1990 are displayed: one at the American Air Museum at the Imperial War Museum Duxford and several at the Royal Armouries, Fort Nelson. Another was displayed at the Royal Artillery Museum, Woolwich, until 2016.

name: Fifth Generation Computer Systems, 1982–1992
description: Japan's programme to build machines that could reason with logic and handle natural language. It ended in 1992.
failedFuture: Machines that would reason in logic and understand language: a 'fifth generation' of computers launched by Japan's MITI in 1982 with the ICOT institute. The promised intelligence did not arrive.
source: Wikipedia, "Fifth generation computer". Referencia primaria por confirmar.

presentEffect.text: Wikipedia says the project 'contributed greatly' to concurrent logic programming: its language KL1 was based on Kazunori Ueda's Guarded Horn Clauses, inspired by Ehud Shapiro's Concurrent Prolog. Its themes are being reinterpreted in multi-core processors and massively parallel computing, and its archives are held at AIST and the Ueda Laboratory.

name: Hermes spaceplane, 1987–1992
description: The European crewed spaceplane Hermes, approved by ESA in November 1987 to carry three astronauts to orbit on Ariane 5. Cancelled in 1992; no vehicle was built.
failedFuture: Europe's own route to orbit with crews, meant to serve a station in space. After repeated delays and cost overruns the project was cancelled, and Europe never flew a crewed spacecraft of its own.
source: ESA, "History: Hermes spaceplane, 1987".

presentEffect.text: More than 200,000 people expressed interest, but finalist Joseph Roche said only 2,761 completed the application, a figure Mars One later confirmed.
